utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday. I would like to greet all those present in the courtroom, as well as the accused, the counsels, the distinguished members of the Office of the Prosecution, as well as all those assisting us in the courtroom. Would the counsel of Mr. Pusic like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Could we please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Could you tell me your name, family name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Gorjanc, 15 March 1943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation or position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment, I am a retired officer of the Slovenian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are a retired officer of the Yugoslav Army. Which rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to repeat. I am a retired colonel of the Slovenian Army, and I did, indeed, serve in the Yugoslav Army. So my rank is that of a colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before a court or is this the first time you have testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the oath which will be put before you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you're an expert witness for the Defence of General Petkovic. You will be testifying for the following two weeks. Since you're under oath, you are not to have any contact with General Petkovic's Defence. Hence, you will not be telling anyone about what's happening within the courtroom, and you may not meet Ms. Alaburic, neither the other counsels. She must have explained that. You will be answering her questions. She will be submitting documents to you in binders, binders which are near your feet, and the usher will be giving them to you later on. Once she is done with her questions, the other accuseds' counsels may ask you questions. The four Judges in front of you will also certainly be asking questions to you as well. And at the end of all these questions, the Office of the Prosecutor on your right-hand side may have -- or will be asking you questions in the context of their cross-examination, and you will notice that the form of questions will be different from the questions asked by General Petkovic's Defence or by the Judges, for that matter, because the Prosecutor is entitled to cross-examine you asking leading questions. To those questions, you're supposed to answer, Yes, No, or, I don't know, and you will be waiting for further questions by the Prosecution if they want you to elaborate. I'm telling you this because we've had problems with witnesses, surprised at the fact that the Prosecutor just wanted, Yes, or, No, for an answer, but that's it. These are the rules of the game and the rules and the practice. You may have your own opinion about it, but this is what it is, and I prefer to tell you this up front to preclude any problems. So please answer the questions that are asked to you. If you do not understand the question, do not hesitate to the person who's asked that question to rephrase or to repeat it. We'll be working for sessions of one hour and a half, but if during the session you feel unwell, don't hesitate to raise your hand so that we can stop right away. This is what I had to say for the proceedings to run smoothly, in the interest of justice. On this note, I would like to give the floor to Ms. Alaburic, whom I would like to greet again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you. Good morning, Mr. Gorjanc. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution, the other Defence teams, and everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gorjanc, let's talk about the language in this courtroom, and let's inform the Trial Chamber how you speak the languages of the former Yugoslavia. What is your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: My mother tongue is Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And as for the languages spoken in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, what other languages do you speak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I speak more or less all the former Yugoslav languages, especially Bosnian and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to inform you that our interpreters speak all the languages from the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and I believe even if you add a Slovenian word, if there is a slip of the tongue on your part, our interpreters will understand that without any problems, and if there are any problems, we will all make sure that our Judges are conveyed your thought precisely. So, Your Honours, for the next ten days in this courtroom, the language that will be spoken here is something that I would call B/C/S/S. The last S stands for "Slovenian." Mr. Gorjanc, if you want to say something in Slovenian, you can do that without any hesitations. Mr. Gorjanc, let's first inform the Trial Chamber about your educational background. I'm going to lead you through those questions, and I hope my learned friends are not going to object to that because they can already find that in your curriculum vitae. I'm going to read back to you what you listed in your CV, in terms of your educational background, and I would like to ask you to make, perhaps correct, or confirm all that. You completed the Military Academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After that, you completed the Command Staff School?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After that, you completed the Political School of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After that, you completed the war school or, rather, the School of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After that, you attended a course in national defence, which was a higher form of education, in a national -- in All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And after that, you attended several short courses in state security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's all that we need to know about your military education. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, in the former Yugoslavia and in the JNA, was there a possibility for an officer to attend continuous education, in terms of any aspect that was important for the functioning of the army and the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And as far as your civilian educational background is concerned, let's see what you did. You dropped out of the School of Politics in Sarajevo because you started attending the Command Staff School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You attended post-graduate studies at the School of Political Sciences in Belgrade, but you dropped out because you were transferred to Postojna, which is in Slovenia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A few words about your professional background, only the most important highlights. As a JNA officer, you served in the following places: Knin, Benkovac, Sarajevo, after that in Slovenia in several places there, and finally in Uzice in Serbia; did I mention all of them, Mr. Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the highest rank you achieved in the JNA was -- or, rather, the highest function was the chief of the Corps Staff in Uzice between 1988 and 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In August 1991, you left the JNA and you went to Slovenia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since the war in Slovenia was in June 1991, that would mean that during that war you were a member of the JNA in Uzice, in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, tell us, were you satisfied with your work in the JNA and with your life in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How come you left the JNA, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Since Slovenia became an independent state, and pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY, the JNA withdrew from the territory of Slovenia. I believe that it was my obligation, as a Slovenian, to join the Slovenian Army, and that's why I left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And before that moment, did the JNA really stay an army of all Yugoslav peoples or did it change?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Until the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and counsel please make breaks. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: And wait. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to my question. Did the JNA remain at that moment, at the moment when the war broke out in Slovenia, an army of all Yugoslav peoples and national minorities or did it change? Can you now give us your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: After the conflict in Slovenia, the Yugoslav People's Army changed its character and became not only an army of all peoples, but of only a few or some peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a follow-up question. When you were in the Army of Yugoslavia, were you a member of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why have you not said so in your CV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you will find it there. I did put it there, that I was a member of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you told us that the JNA had transformed into an army of some peoples. Which peoples were those?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The Officer Staff of the army were 60 per cent officers and non-commissioned officers from Serbia and Montenegro. When the armed conflict started in Slovenia, members of the Slovenian ethnicity left the army, and most of the officers and non-commissioned officers of Croatian ethnicity also left the JNA, as well as some Muslim officers and Albanian officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In documents that you mentioned in paragraph 5 of your report, you emphasise that you did not desert from the JNA. Could you please [as interpreted] why you worded that section in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The Presidency of Slovenia invited all officers not to participate in the aggression against Slovenia. Later on, some accepted that as an invitation to desert the JNA. I didn't want that because I was under obligation, and when I -- my departure was approved, when it was -- when I was given the green light to leave, I left only then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you said "obligation," did you mean the oath that you took?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, the oath that I took when I started education at the Military Academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, after that, after your return to Slovenia, did you start working in the Slovenian Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your CV, it says that you were the chief of the Department for Education and Training in the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence, and after that you worked at the Centre for Strategic Studies, firstly as an adviser and then for a brief period of time as a director. Then you were director at the Centre of Military Schools of the Slovenian Army. After that, you were a lecturer in tactics and operations at the Command Staff Academy of the Slovenian Army. And according to your own words, you were pensioned off in May 1999. Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My next question refers to your political activity. His Honour Judge Antonetti has already asked you something about that, but let me ask you something about your membership in the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia between 1986 and 1990. Let me ask you this: The best-known congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was the one that was abandoned or there was a walk-out by the Croatian/Slovenian delegations in 1990. Did you attend that congress?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend that congress.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you leave or did you stay after the Slovenian and Croatian delegations walked out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I stayed because I was a member of the delegation of the League of Communists of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, were you active in Slovenia's Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It deals with human rights; right? It deals with human rights; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you specify the period you were a member?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I still am, as a matter of fact. I'm a member of the board. However, I'm no longer as active as I used to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since when have you been active in the Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: 2001 was the starting year.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your CV, you say that you were a military commentator, an analyst. You published quite a number of articles and works of research. Is the information reflected in your CV correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You additionally amended something about the drafts of your expert reports in two different cases before this Tribunal. At first, you said that those were public reports, whereas later on you clarified that those were mere draft reports that you never completed and, therefore, never published; is that right, Mr. Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes. The mistake is all mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first what cases you were talking about. What ICTY cases?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The Kordic case and the Kolundzija case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the other case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Kolundzija, the one before it, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll correct that later on. How did your involvement in the Kolundzija case end?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Eventually I was not called to testify because there had been a plea agreement between the Prosecution and the accused, or at least that's what I was told at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By Your Honour's leave, I would like to move into private session now. I would like to ask the witness some questions about his involvement in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, do you personally know Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, we met 35 years ago in Postojna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you actually meet or did you work together?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: We worked together in the same barracks for six years.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is your impression of General Petkovic? What was he like 35 years ago, except for more hair on his head, no doubt?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: There wasn't that much more, to be perfectly frank. He was a young lieutenant, young captain, and the commander of an elite unit, a division, anti-armour battery, as a matter of fact. This was one of the best units in the entire division. It was also the strike force that the JNA used for anti-armour combat, the best such unit within that division. I knew him as an exceptionally composed, calm, and responsible officer. I did not work directly with him, but we were in contact a number of times. At the time, I was also deputy barracks commander. In my capacity, I was receiving reports from the officers then on duty, and among their number was also the then Captain Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you also happen to be a Praljak Defence military expert. Let me ask you this question: Did you personally know General Praljak as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: No, I only knew him from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mr. Gorjanc, I'll be asking you a number of questions now about the way in which your expert report was drafted. To begin with, who typed it up for our benefit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You can write?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, I can both use a typewriter and a PC.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When did you learn to use a PC?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: When I was the chief of the Corps Staff in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During our meetings, Mr. Gorjanc, you never used a single sheet of paper. You always brought your computer, nevertheless. Can you tell me how you organised the whole thing for yourself on your computer in order to be able to track down all the documents immediately and follow everything that was going on, document-wise, facing these enormous amounts of paperwork?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I've developed a system of gathering required materials. Everything that's written, I immediately transform into a digital format, be it an image or a PDF document, and then I make excerpts from certain relevant documents or sections of documents that I believe to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you include as part of your report certain maps that are obviously computer generated. Can you tell me who produced those maps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I produced them myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Briefly, how did the Praljak Defence and the Petkovic Defence get in touch with you? Who was the first to call you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic was the first to call me. We had a brief encounter not far from my holiday cottage. We had lunch together, and he simply asked me whether I was willing to come on board and work with your team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who took it on from there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: You were the only person that I then was still in touch with after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, can you roughly give us a year or time when we first got in touch with you and we started working together?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I think it was around Easter time 2007. We met no more than a month later. I think it was actually during the summer break. And then we would meet at regular intervals over the several months that followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From our very first meeting, what was the one thing that was entirely certain as to what the substance of your expert report should be or should reflect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Primarily, the importance of Central Bosnia and Northern Herzegovina in the war, as well as All-People's Defence as it applied in the previous state or country and as it panned out during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During our brief meetings -- or, rather, where did we meet?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Once, I believe, at the Holiday Hotel in Zagreb. I'm not that familiar with the center of Zagreb, so I asked you to meet me along one of the roads leading into the city. And then I think I came to your office in Zagreb about three times total after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During our meetings -- or, rather, how long were our meetings, normally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The first one took an hour, perhaps, no more than that. Afterwards, we would normally talk for two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about your impression of those meetings? Was I seeking your professional opinion on any documents or developments of military relevance to this case, or did we, as a rule, discuss the case generally, in a general way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: My impression was you were trying to find out how familiar I was with the subject matter as a whole. It wasn't that we discussed any specifics.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, when I explained your brief to you, in terms of drafting your expert report and when you produced the reports, did you work independently and did you present nothing but your own independent opinions, or was there anyone who tried to exert pressure on you to say this or to say that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I was entirely independent, and there was no one trying to channel my work or monitor my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there any demands that were made by our Defence for you to alter or change any of your opinions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your expert report has chapters or paragraphs that are numbered. How come?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I wrote this, for the most part, as one produces a thesis at university. I subdivided this into chapters, and you asked me to do just that for ease of handling here in this courtroom. So I assigned numbers to the different chapters and paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, what were the documents that you used for your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Initially, I was working based on what I had previously experienced in the Kordic case, and then at a later stage I went back to you for further documents, especially as original documents were concerned, although most of the original documents I was able to track down on the web, specifically Mr. Praljak's web site.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about various memoirs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: For the most part, those were my books from earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you wrote about the doctrine of All-People's Defence, you were using various regulations; right? We lawyers always find it very interesting, how someone who is not, by profession, a lawyer should be using regulations and books of regulations. I must ask you several questions in that regard. Were you familiar with the laws and regulations covering the Defence Sector at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: By all means, I was, yes. Being in command of the units that I was and my job in the army required a detailed knowledge of regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about your involvement in Slovenia? Were you actively involved in drafting the defence-related regulations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, I was consulted, and I provided certain opinions on the first-draft Defence Law which was adopted in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One final question about these methodological remarks. In your opinion, in order to understand the Defence Law, is it not necessary to actually be familiar with the subject matter, the actual thing, defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, because laws are always based on practice, in order to change that practice somehow in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, let's move on to your report. I would kindly ask the usher to hand over to the witness the expert report and all the documents that have been prepared for him. Let's start with chapter 4, which is "Wartime Army." In that chapter, Mr. Gorjanc, you describe two types of wartime armies, one which is created from a peacetime army and the second one which is an ad hoc wartime army. Could you please tell us, just in a very few brief outlines, what is the notion of an ad hoc wartime army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: An ad hoc wartime army is created under the conditions and principles of the non-existence of a state and the peacetime organisation of the defence system of such a state. It is mostly created under the conditions of civil liberation, inter-religious, inter-ethnic and inter-racial conflicts. It is a chaotic process, at the beginning the main goal being to resist either the occupying force, the existing government. And first the units are small, engaged in mostly guerrilla and terrorist actions. With time, those units gain support among the population and gradually grow into bigger groups, with the final result being an army with its system of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, the military expert for the Prosecution, Andrew Pringle, said before this Trial Chamber that it should take several years for the -- for a proper army to be created, and that was recorded on page 24246. Tell us, please, Mr. Gorjanc, would you be able to agree with Mr. Pringle's assertion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, but it depends on the level of threat that the country faced, the level of preparations, and the level of unity of the population to support such an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the organisation of an ad hoc army, how would this look from a center -- from a top, in a centralised way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It would be easier, it would be much simpler, because in such a case there would be a state, there would be some tangible conditions for its creation, there is an officer staff, and then all you have to do is to form commands. And you also have a large number of reserve officers that had been trained previously from which you can create larger-size units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If a wartime army is created in a decentralised way, could you describe the situation for us then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In that case, as I've already told you, the process starts with small units which are not linked up without the unity of command, without any communication among those units. They have just one link, and that's their ideology, and the ideology boils down to a countering the enemy, and it's a much harder way to create a wartime army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, if you were to compare a decentralised army as opposed to a centralised army, what would you say? Which chain of command is established -- established in a faster and more complete way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It would certainly be in an organised and centralised way. The chain of command is actually established even before any units are established, whereas in an ad hoc army which is formed in a decentralised way, it is first units, then commands at lower units, and finally commands at the highest levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me if I interrupt. On line -- on page 21, the first lines, you have said, Mr. Gorjanc, that, I quote: "It depends on the level of threat that the country faced, the level of preparations, and the population to support such an army." Now, I would be grateful if you could explain in which way it depends. The greater the threat, what? What is the relation in these mechanisms that you intimate? I hope I made myself understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the threat is higher, which would mean that the enemy is stronger, then it is more difficult to establish such an army, especially because of the lack of the necessary support on the part of the population due to the repressive measures undertaken by the enemy. However, the enemy repressive measures at a certain point in time can even stimulate the population to put up more resistance and join the units faster.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, Judge Trechsel's question was a bit different. I believe that the question referred to the time that was necessary for a wartime army to be organised, because in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think the witness understood me quite well, and he gave an answer which I consider a correct and valuable answer. If I may sum up, you first said that the greater the threat, the greater the difficulties, but it may also be that the greater threat fosters more willingness with a people to get together and to make efforts which would facilitate an army. So in a way, there is a certain ambivalence, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Alaburic, and thank you for your efforts, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now summarise, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I'm sorry. This is an occasion, I think, to ask my own question to the witness. Witness, you quote the expert of the Prosecution, Andrew Pringle, about the number of years which were necessary to establish an army. Could you specify what is this number of years, according to you, and if it is the same in all cases? Because I'm thinking for the moment for the different armies of the ex-Yugoslavia, the Slovenian, the Croatian Army, and the others. Those are armies which recuperated officers and soldiers which were trained by the JNA, and this gives you an impression of an army which starts from scratch; it's not the case? I'm talking about the training of the officers and the soldiers, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The creation of different armies in different states on the ground of the former Yugoslavia is very different. If I may say so, the HVO, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina [as interpreted], were liberation armies, and they have some joint characteristics in terms of how they were created. All of those armies that were formed on the ground of the former Yugoslavia have one thing in common; all their members, or most of them, had been trained in the former JNA as conscripts and during manoeuvres as members of the reserve force. Also, some of the officers had been trained by the JNA, both active through regular education, as well as reserve officers who were trained as reserve officers in appropriate schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. But precisely because these officers were very well trained, and a great number of the soldiers were also, I would like to create a parallel -- make a parallel between the army of a young state, which is just starting from scratch. What is, according to you, the number of years which would be necessary to reach the level of a normal army? With the case, for instance, of the ex-Yugoslavia or the case of an African army or an independent state, would there be no difference in the number of years necessary to do this, to establish this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such a case when a new state is created, a state which doesn't have any trained officer staff, that process would take much longer. A recent history shows, especially when it comes to the liberation movements in Africa, that those movements took ten years before they were able to create armies that would be able to secure them independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. For the moment, I will stop there, but we will see a bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am listening very carefully to what you tell us, and sometimes when you use a word, I wonder. A while ago, you were speaking about the HVO army and the BiH Army, that they were liberation armies, and when you said that, I wondered, What does the witness mean? Does he mean that the JNA occupied the Bosnia-Herzegovina Republic, Croatia, Slovenia, and that when there was the dismantling of Yugoslavia, there was a liberation which took place? Is this what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The JNA was not an occupying army, although politicians proclaimed it an occupying army. It was a state army for as long as it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then why do you qualify the HVO as a liberation army, and BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't remember having said the liberation armies. If I did, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was the one who was supposed to intervene to correct the record, because it's the record that creates problems. On page 23, line 21, here it reads that the witness is speaking about the HVO and the BiH Army, which were liberation armies. The witness was speaking about the HVO and about the Liberation Army of Kosovo. The witness never mentioned the BiH Army. I was going to correct that, but I did not think that it would create any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you see, I'm listening to every word. There was a translation problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: However, I would like to arrive at a simple answer in response to Judge Trechsel's questions. If there are no objections, I would like to lead the witness. Is it possible that due to the circumstances and wartime conditions and special requirements at the time that was necessary for the formation of a war army was actually shorter than a few years that have just been mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, but a minimum of -- a minimum would be one year.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now continue comparing two armies, the one that is created in a decentralised way and another one which is created in a centralised way. What would you say about the influence of local authorities on the army in these two different types of wartime armies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In an army that is created through centralisation, when there is a state, when there is a supreme command as the primary command, and where there is a body of law, constitution laws, decrees, and so on and so forth, and there is also a system which goes from the lowest level to the highest level of civilian authorities, in such a case an army is exclusively in the function of the performance of such civilian authorities, which is the defence of the country together with the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the influence of local authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Local authorities, in principle, when it comes to a centralised army, don't play any role and don't exert any influence on military units, even at the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about in a decentralised army or an army that was created in a decentralised way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In such a case, the first units that are created are small units at local levels, and they are usually supported, created, and logistically supported by local communities, and those local communities try to exert influence over those units for as long as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, given your military experience and knowledge, would you tell us, if a municipality is funding its own military unit, would you, as a military commander, be able to estimate that the military -- that the municipal authority will exert influence on that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Of course, because they pay the bill, they foot the bill, and they will not give up on the influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given your knowledge and experience, and also the familiarity with the events on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, would you say that the media and public opinion in an environment exert influence on the behaviour of soldiers in that environment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this part of your expert report, you explain the components of a wartime army as manoeuvre and territorial components. Could you please briefly explain? What is it that you speak about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The manoeuvre component has the purpose of carrying out combat operations throughout the territory of a country or even in enemy territory. Territorial Defence, on the other hand, serves the purpose of defence and protection of the immediate environment where it is set up. Another purpose is to monitor the territory throughout, in exceptional cases to carry out combat operations against the enemy along the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, can you please look at the first document now in the set of documents; not the expert report, but the other binder, which is the first binder with documents. This is P907, 907, which is an exhibit. This is a report from December 1992 by the Chief of the Main Staff. At this point in time, I would like to go to page 3. For the benefit of the Chamber, this is the last paragraph in item 3 of the report. We see some figures there concerning HVO units. It says that at that time, the HVO had a total of 45.000 men. As for the professional units, there were 855 members. Mr. Gorjanc, let us assume that the 855 men were involved in manoeuvre units, and the remainder, up to 45.000, were with territorial units. What would you say? What does that tell you about the character of the HVO as an army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: If we bear in mind the fact that there were all these brigades bearing the name of their native areas in which they were established, one can conclude with certainty and for the most part these are territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given the function of territorial units, what would you be led to conclude, based on this document, regarding the character of the HVO as an army? Was it established in order to conquer territory, to defend territory, or was it organisation-neutral?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Given the fact that it was organised mostly based on a territorial principle, I assumed that its fundamental task was to defend its territory within its own municipality, the municipality in which it was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 24 of your expert report, line 5, you mentioned the concept of immediate front-line, you talk about army activities outside the immediate front-line. Can you define that concept for us? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The immediate front-line covers an area in which certain units directly involved in combat are operating, units being used for quick interventions along the front-line. In a specific area and given the nature of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the range would be between three and five kilometres from the confrontation line into one's own territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the deployment was like, the front-line and then the three- to five-kilometre belt, and then all the way behind the lines? What exactly goes on there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In a theatre of war like that, within the three- to five-range kilometre, you have mostly battalion level units and direct firing support for those units, 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars. Further behind, you can have the artillery weapons with a greater range. But for the most part, you have soldiers resting, or operative reserves, as we call them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 25, the last bullet, you conclude that it is impossible to carry out large-scale offensive operations with units of the territorial component without previous thorough training from the individual to the unit at the operational level. Can you briefly explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: There are several joint tactical units taking part in operation, at least two to three brigades with appropriate artillery support, and these units must be properly trained to operate as a single entity. It would even be good if they were able to operate as a single entity within the operative unit. You cannot defeat an enemy brigade if you're using a single brigade of your own. The general principle is the ratio should be 1:3 in favour of the attacking party, attacking side, in some cases even a greater ratio than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You react here, Mr. Gorjanc, to a decision by Enver Hadzihasanovic, commander of the 3rd Corps Command. The document number is 4D1473, 1473. This is the second document in that binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to come back to a question which was asked to you by Ms. Alaburic, but she didn't elaborate on her question. Still, I do think that it is a question which is fundamental for the case. There are, of course, quite a few fundamental questions, but this one is even more fundamental. Ms. Alaburic highlights the fact that the HVO is a territorial army, and you said that the names -- that the brigades had the names of the municipalities. And we were shown a document to the effect that there are 45.000 soldiers in the HVO and a professional branch of 855 soldiers, among which 85 officers. Now, you know as well as I do that in the HVO there were professional units. Now, with an 800-strong unit, is it possible to carry out large-scale military operations in a territory such as Bosnia-Herzegovina, to take control of these territories or to annex them? Do you think it's possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professional units would certainly not be able to establish control. Nevertheless, when I spoke of the territorial army, I said their main objective was to monitor their territory. All these brigades were established on a territorial basis. That's a fact. Therefore, they monitor the territory of their own municipality or municipalities in which they were established. Along these lines, you could say that the HVO was establishing control over some of the territory, whereas the unit that was used for activities throughout the territory would not have been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Replace "800 individual units" by "a 800-soldier unit."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, when you say control --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Soldier unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- of the territory, what exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: That means controlling traffic, controlling any population movement, protecting features and facilities of particular importance, and control over any potential incursions by enemy forces into the territory, or possibly repelling any incursions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If my conclusion is right, these are military functions which are important in order to defend the territory of a municipality. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So when you say "control," did you have in mind other functions, such as upholding public law and order or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: No, "control" in the military sense alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this context, meaning no offensive actions could be launched through these territorial component units, we see your reaction to this decision by the 3rd Corps Command. This is 4D1473, 4D1473. Mr. Gorjanc, could you clarify the meaning of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In the memoirs of the commander of the Lasva Operative Group, General Alagic, I noticed something which I didn't mention here. When the 305th Jajce Brigade was involved along the Visoko front for the first time as a whole, as a single entity, this proved to be very successful, and then I went on looking for a document which I then found on the web, on Mr. Praljak's web site, the document being a decision by the commander of the 3rd Corps for the setting-up camp. He took all the units to a certain area in Central Bosnia in order to have a joint training exercise, and in order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Let me repeat only briefly that please kindly indicate in which binder can we find that article, in particular the 4D1473 document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I forgot to explain how the binders are organised. You have a small binder containing the expert report and then three binders containing documents which we shall be discussing with this witness. The documents are organised based on the chapters of the expert report. There is a blue slip of paper separating them, there is a title every time, and the documents are ordered in a sequence that I shall be following as I examine the witness. If I run out of time, I may have to skip something, but I'll always give you advanced notice of that. Therefore, we are now dealing with binder number 1, and this is the second document in that binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, could you please continue explaining the importance of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The Command of the 3rd Corps decided to use all of their forces, including the territorial units, the municipal staffs, and all of their units, to set up camp in an area in which their units were otherwise partially involved along the front-line, the objective being to raise their stamina, the stamina of soldiers, commanders, members of those units, to strengthen the bonds of trust between them and their general comradeship, as a whole. Previously, it says that there should be a manoeuvre to fool the enemy, in terms of hiding their own intentions of carrying out combat operations. The aim or the objective was to properly train the units for them to be able -- units, the rank of a brigade, in order to perform large-scale combat operations, to train them for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In relation to this, I have two further questions. You said units of the 3rd Corps, as a single entity or as a whole. What exactly does that mean? Does that have to do with the units taking shifts the way the BH Army had been functioning up to that point? What exactly did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: If you look at this notion, you see that the units that were deployed along the front-line would become a form of decisive defence, in terms of defending that line, whereas the other units that were resting in their own respective areas would now come to this area where they were setting up camp, and then they were all -- they were all about to carry out some training together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct? Is this the first time that the army was not working in shifts, but rather they were all together there without rotating, all present in this camp for this round of training? Right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you read a part of this decision about concealing their true intentions, can you tell us what that means to you? How do you interpret this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. The commander, in one portion of the document, says that defence activity will be actively used to inflict the greatest possible losses on the Serbs, the Chetniks, in terms of manpower and equipment. Nevertheless, when I looked up the positions of those units on the camp map, as a soldier I simply couldn't understand why the greatest part of those forces were actually positioned away from the front-line facing the Serbs, stretched along a very broad front facing the Serbs; towards Mount Vlasic, towards Tesanj, towards Tuzla and so on and so forth. As for offensive operations, large-scale offensive operations, as the document states, they would need to join forces along a narrower front and then direct this action at a single target.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was your conclusion, according to what you saw on the map? What was the brunt of the 3rd Corps attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Given the deployment, I would say that the target was to cut off communications in the Lasva and Lepenica Valleys, which means between Travnik and Vitez and Vitez and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gorjanc, could you please tell us something about -- about army taking shifts? You've explained that very well. What matters to us here is the following question: According to your knowledge and experience, army taking shifts, does it reduce or increase militarily in discipline?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In any case, it reduces military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: One-third of the units, in principle, I'm talking in principle and the ratios could be different, in principle one-third is on the front-line, engaging the enemy. The other third is in the vicinity of the front-line, in the facilities or on other premises, and one-third is at home, on furlough, in neighbouring places, and this is especially typical of a territorial army. When it comes to that one-third that is at home, in factual matters the commander cannot exert effective control over their behaviour as soldiers and citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, could you please try, in view of your military experience and knowledge, could you please try and tell us if everybody knows what the effect on military discipline and an army taking shifts has? How come that somebody will decide to organise their army in such a way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It happens when the opposing party also applies that type of warfare under adverse weather conditions and other conditions, when the intensity of combat is not that high, when there are no forthcoming offensives on the part of the enemy side, and also it has a positive effect on the morale of the fighters and the population alike. And, thirdly, this reduces the cost of logistics, the accommodation of soldiers, and if they spend time at home they can look after their households, their family members, and the local commune as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you have an army that is not organised as an army taking shifts, do you have to have barracks or some other facility where the troops would be billeted, where they would spend nights?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It would be desirable to have barracks or facilities where the troops could not only be billeted and sleep, but also where they could have some sort of a normal life, where they could have washing facilities, entertainment facilities, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given your good knowledge of the facilities of the JNA in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you please tell us where the barracks were located in the territory of North Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In the territory of North Herzegovina, there were just two such facilities, one in Mostar and the other in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 37 of your expert report, Mr. Gorjanc, you're trying to explain the difference between warfaring in one's own territory and warfaring in the territory of a different state, of another state. Could you please briefly explain the difference to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The difference arises primarily from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to paragraph 37, I would like to ask a follow-up question. I was really interested in what you said on a third facing the front-line, a third as a reserve, or a third at home -- and a third at home.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, and a third at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I have these three figures in mind. Let's assume, and this is a hypothesis, let's assume there is an offensive action, and I underline "offensive," so you have a third facing the Serbs on the front-line. Knowing this, how can the HVO carry out an offensive action if you have a third of the soldiers at home and a third in reserve? How can the HVO solve that problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be exceptionally difficult, especially to organise an offensive on a large scale. You can organise an attack by recruiting reservists close to the front-line, and those troops who are at home are not easy to gather if they are at home, if it's not coming up to the time when they are supposed to return to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that with the so-called system of territorial army, is it impossible, from a military point of view, to carry out large-scale military operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's impossible, if you're talking about a large-scale operation which would require the engagement of an entire brigade, if not more people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'm sure we'll have an opportunity to come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, and then we will bring that chapter to an end. In paragraph 37, Mr. Gorjanc, you're trying to point out the difference between waging a war in one's own territory as opposed to waging a war in the territory of a different state. Could you please explain the difference to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The difference arises from the fact how the civilian authorities act. In one's own territory, where there is an already-arranged system of power which is implemented and regulated, military units and military commanders are duty-bound to respect those regulations and show such an attitude towards civilian authorities. The attitude, that means mutual trust, mutual cooperation, and mutual respect. In case when you are in the process of taking another territory or liberating one's own territory after it had been under the jurisdiction or military occupation of another army, then the military commander has all the powers to take over some of the authorities of the civilian authorities, and in that case we call such a commander a military government. However, even in such cases he has to cooperate with the authorities that had previously existed, if such authorities are cooperative, if such authorities are of assistance to that commander. If those authorities are hostile, he has the right to remove and bring in his own people. If we are talking about the liberation of the formerly -- of former territories, he has such powers, but he has to cede power to the previously-elected authorities or bring in his own people that had been appointed by the central authorities of the mother state.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Gorjanc, how is this done by the American Army in Iraq, for example, or another state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Every American division has a brigade for civilian affairs. That brigade has the task to establish civilian authorities in the territory that the American Army takes. That brigade has, on its strength, different experts, mostly lawyers, administrative experts, experts in the matters of economy, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What you have just told us, Mr. Gorjanc, is that something that arises from the military doctrine as a rule that is applicable to all situations, or would that be something specific for Bosnia or Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: No, this is what every military in the world does, with the caveat that the American Army is specific in that case, owing to the fact that it has a special unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I have finished with this part of the expert report, maybe this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing starts again. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, we shall now move on to the doctrine of All-People's Defence. But before that, we will also be talking about laws regulating the Yugoslav People's Army. But let's clarify your answer to the as to whether the Yugoslav People's Army at one point became an aggressor in any of the territories of the former Yugoslavia. If I understood you correctly, you said that the Yugoslav People's Army could not have been an aggressor in the territory of Yugoslavia for as long as Yugoslavia existed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That would then mean that after the break-up of Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia could have been an aggressor in some of the parts of the former Yugoslavia; am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: That was after the withdrawal from Slovenia, the JNA only by name, but in factual terms it was no longer -- it was no longer the Yugoslav People's Army. It was not even the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was created subsequently. In that sense, I don't think that the JNA was an occupator [as interpreted] anyway. However, the remainder that withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia behaved as an occupator [as interpreted] -- as an occupying force in Bosnia-Herzegovina is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Gorjanc, when did the so-called Yugoslav People's Army withdraw from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It started withdrawing from Slovenia on the 18th of July, and it withdrew completely on the 26th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then consider that after the dates that you've just mentioned, the JNA no longer existed and that the remains of the JNA could have been an occupying force in one of the parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that clarification. Your Honours, we will start this section with a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thought this was a bit fast. If Slovenia is off the former Yugoslavia, does that mean that the rest does not exist as a mutilated SFRY? You seem to say Slovenia off, Yugoslavia broken, doesn't exist anymore, and I wonder whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not a lawyer, especially not an expert for international law. However, in my view, personally, the JNA stopped existing and Yugoslavia stopped existing because it did not contain Slovenia, and Croatia also declared its independence at the same time. So it was a rump Yugoslavia, as they call it, but it was no longer Yugoslavia with its former six republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is different. If you say it was rump Yugoslavia, I can accept that. The question, of course, then arises whether this still means that an aggression is possible, an aggression is not possible. But as you state, you are not a lawyer, and this is essentially, I think, a legal question. I will not insist that you answer at all. I think you have done as good as you can be expected to do. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I absolutely agree with you. I wanted the witness to provide us with his own opinion on that. And we know exactly when Yugoslavia broke up and what was happening at the time, so I don't think we should have any problem with that. Your Honours, the section about All-People's Defence is something that we would like to start with a video-clip. If you will allow me, I'm not going to inform you in advance who is depicted in the video-clip. I would like to ask the witness to tell us that, and then we would provide some explanations as to what the whole thing is all about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We are doing everything to make any interference with Yugoslavia impossible, even after me, because anybody who would think that after my departure Yugoslavia could be weakened from inside and that it is now in danger to become prey for some invasion from the Soviet part, I don't believe in that. Yugoslavia has a firm unity, regardless of its multi-nationality. Today, Yugoslavia has, it could be said, one of the strongest militaries in Europe. Then we also have All-People's Defence with a huge number of people, and we enacted into law that everybody must be faithful to the defence of the country and thereon. "Yugoslavia can deploy 8 million people in the battle-field, and 8 million is not a joke, especially considering that those people are Yugoslav, who are accustomed to being on a war path."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my associate, Davor Lazic, tells me that the translation or interpretation did not start from the very beginning, but I don't think we should re-run the video-clip. I would like to draw your attention that the film is in electronic courtroom under number 4D1733.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would appreciate if that information was furnished before the video-clip was played.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, a question for you. Do you recognise the person on the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I did not have the image on my screen, but I recognised it by voice. This is Josip Broz Tito. He was my commander for a number of years. He was talking about 8 million people that he could arm at any one time. At that time in Yugoslavia, the units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence of all republics numbered about 2.400.000 people, and the figure of 8 million refers to the entire population, able-bodied men, ranging in age from 16 to 60. That would be the approximate explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this statement dated 1978, just before his visit to the US, his statement to an American journalist, he mentioned the doctrine of All-People's Defence. What about these 8 million potential soldiers? Does that have anything to do with the doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, in every way. Under the Constitution, the entire population, those who were able-bodied and able to resist in an armed way, the number would have grown significantly even compared to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean the women, too?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, them, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance, please. If Mr. Gorjanc's monitor can be switched to e-court. I now understand that he didn't see the video-clip, so the monitor is probably in the wrong mode.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Gorjanc, could you please explain when the doctrine of All-People's Defence was first established?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The doctrine was first discussed in the autumn of 1968, following the incursion carried out by the Warsaw Pact powers into Czechoslovakia. Yugoslavia then felt that it, too, was at risk from the same forces. Facing that kind of power and in that kind of environment, a textbook army, such as the JNA, would not have been able to withstand an aggression. The doctrine was then adopted and became part of the Constitution in 1974, after which it was elaborated in a systematic way. The first documents about the doctrine in writing were first released in 1973. The doctrine was complete, you might say, in terms of the theory, by 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, were you, too, involved in the creation of that doctrine and its implementation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The implementation, yes, sure thing, but as for the creation of that doctrine, at a lower level, the level of my command, starting with battalion level and company/platoon level corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in the briefest possible terms, what the essence of the doctrine of All-People's Defence might be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The substance of the doctrine is about pooling together all the resources of a country, in this case Yugoslavia, for the purpose of defending its sovereignty and integrity, meaning the armed forces and all the other players involved in armed as well as non-armed resistance and any other activities supporting that resistance, regardless of the age and sex of those involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will speak about that in greater detail when we come to the regulations. Now, paragraph 44, if we could please move on to that, you talk about committees for ONO and DSZ, which is short for "All-People's Defence" and "Social Self-Protection," ONO and DSZ, "Social Self-Protection." Mr. Gorjanc, could you tell us what these committees were, headed by who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: These committees for ONO and DSZ were a form of political control exercised by the League of Communists, the party, over the entire defence system. The committees comprised representatives or leaders of various socio-political organisations in certain environments, as well as municipal presidents, a municipal executive board president, the head of the Internal Affairs Secretariat, the commander of the Territorial Defence, and by virtue of his position, also the commander of whichever JNA unit happened to be in a certain specific area. These committees had within their remit the organisation of defence in a certain area. In case the defence wasn't functioning, it was their job to take any measures available to them to set up forms of resistance. Whenever that wasn't possible, they would take charge of commanding the defence of that area. The committee would normally be headed by the president or the secretary of the League of Communists in a certain local area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Speaking of these committees for ONO and DSZ, if you tried to compare these to bodies that came into existence in the early 1990s in certain parts of the former Yugoslavia, and I believe that was the case in Slovenia as well, which particular body could you compare these committees to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In Slovenia, we had something that we referred to as coordination, ranging from the local communes and then on to municipalities in the republic itself. The coordination body was headed by the prime minister, who was also the president of the party in power. In other areas, such as Bosnia and Croatia, in particular, they had something they called crisis staffs at municipal levels or district levels. And that's about as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You say that these committees were also organised at the level of local communes and municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge, these crisis staffs that were set up in the early 1990s across Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were organised at municipal levels, too, or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were organised at the municipal level, headed by a party president or a mayor normally from the party that won the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A hypothetical question. Were someone to tell you that these crisis staffs in municipalities across Bosnia-Herzegovina had influence over military units in these same municipal territories, would you believe that this had anything to do with how the All-People's Defence committees had been working previously?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The way they conducted their business was almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, thank you. Mr. Gorjanc, let's look at the first document after the blue paper. I think the documents are separated by a blue sheet of paper. 1D2976, 1D2976. This is the Constitution of the SFRY. At this point in time, we will be looking at Article 240, paragraph 3. Article 240, paragraph 3. Can you please read this article, Mr. Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: "Each citizen participating in resistance against the enemy in an armed way is a member of the armed forces of the SFRY."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, can you now tell us, from the point of view of a citizen, who in the former Yugoslavia would be considered a member of the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Anyone putting up resistance to an attacker, an aggressor in any way, armed or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer? Armed or --

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Armed or not, armed or in another manner. In an armed manner or in another manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question, a follow-up question. I'm reading paragraph 3 of Article 204 [as interpreted], and I put myself -- I place myself in the generalised defence -- people's defence. You have been an officer in the JNA, and you have said that during several years you were in the same barracks as Captain Petkovic. I would like to know, according to your memories, at the level of the JNA were there some orders, or circulars, or instructions which were either written or verbal on possible problems in the ex-republics of Yugoslavia, and trouble, let's say, and where the JNA would have intervened? Has such an assumption or hypothesis has been envisaged or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were no particular instructions regarding that. Nevertheless, the JNA during its existence intervened several times in different areas; Kosovo, first and foremost, when there was unrest. The last such intervention was on the 9th of March, 1991, in Belgrade, when there were the huge nationalist rallies taking place. However, there were no specific instructions regarding that. Back in 1988, sometime in the spring of 1988 - I can't remember the exact date, I was not personally involved in that - a document was produced covering the entire territory, in the sense of involving JNA units in the eventuality of riots, unrest, rallies. This document was produced specifically for Slovenia, and eventually the person who outed this document, published this document, was tried simply because the document was a classified one, a state secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, of course it goes without saying that this document would have been interesting -- particularly interesting, since we don't have this document - maybe we'll have it one day, you never know - that in case of incidents, you spoke about the intervention of the JNA in Kosovo. When there are incidents, trouble, can you consider that a civilian may be potentially a combatant if one applies Article 240 which we are -- which we have here, and if he potentially, he is a combatant, will then the JNA -- can it -- can the JNA arrest him then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The doctrine of All-People's Defence was not meant to be used against one's own citizens, it was meant to be used against an external enemy. In situations involving one's own citizens, it was the civilian police that took action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "an external enemy," Mr. Gorjanc, who exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: One of the states that conceivably could have attacked Yugoslavia at the time. We prepared equally in relation to all of the neighbouring states surrounding us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us try to wrap up Article 240, paragraph 3.
