It follows, based on this article, does it not, that a person putting up armed resistance in defence of his country and another person defending his country in an unarmed way would be equally considered, both of them, as fighters and members of the JNA; is that what the doctrine of All-People's Defence amounted to, in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Article 237 of this same document, it talks about how the defence of the country is an inviolable and inalienable right and duty of the nation's nationalities, working people, and citizens. Let's look at citizens for the time being, Mr. Gorjanc. Given your military expertise and your familiarity with these regulations, what does this mean, the inviolable and inalienable right, in terms of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: "Inviolable and inalienable" means that no one can deny anyone else the right to put up resistance, to resist. No later regulation contradicting the Constitution could be applied in this sense, in the sense of preventing someone from putting up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the next document now, the Law on All-People's Defence. This is 4D1470. You discuss this law in paragraph 54 of your expert report. We'll be looking at some key regulations which I think are material to our understanding of the doctrine of All-People's Defence. To start with, Article 91, Article 91. It reads: "The armed forces make up a single entity and are comprised of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence." And then, in paragraph 2, there is the following provision: "Any citizen who, with weapons or in any other fashion, participates in resistance against the enemy is also considered a member of the armed forces." Mr. Gorjanc, is this the same fundamental provision that we analysed a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the operationalisation of a constitutional provision in the form of a law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to Article 3, defining the notion or the concept of All-People's Defence. Could you please pay particular attention to the concept of all-people's resistance in line 7. It's right there. There are the various forms of all-people's resistance being enumerated there. What is the place of all-people's resistance in the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Resistance, I would say, is the chief component -- the main component of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at Article 17 of the same law. In this article, there are definitions of the basic forms or, rather, the basic rights and duties within the scope of All-People's Defence. Mr. Gorjanc, could you please tell us, what were the basic rights and duties within All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I apologise. The basic rights and duties were the military obligation, the obligation to take part in civil protection, the obligation to fulfill work obligation, to be trained for All-People's Defence, and to meet requisition requirements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the Article 118 of the same law, which regulates the reinforcement of the armed forces. And here it says that: "Units and institutions of All-People's Defence are reinforced," and I'm quoting, "with personnel from the regular and reserve armed forces." Could you please tell us, Mr. Gorjanc, who makes up the regular force, on the one hand, and who makes up the reserve force, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The regular force is composed of active officers of -- or active military personnel, students of military schools, and civilians serving in the armed forces. Soldiers carrying out their military duty are also part of that strength.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what about the reserve -- the reserve armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The reserve armed forces are composed of able-bodied men who had served in the army, those who had regulated their army service in a different way, and female military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's skip the Law on Service in the Armed Forces, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Mr. Gorjanc, I fail to understand this. The title is "Reinforcement of the Armed Forces," and then: "The armed forces shall be reinforced with personnel from the regular armed forces." To me, this reads tautological because the regular armed forces are the armed forces. How do the armed forces reinforce the armed forces? I would be grateful if you could explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the problem arises from the translation or interpretation and that Mr. Gorjanc does not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging from what His Honour has just said, it is a tautology, but it's not about reinforcing forces, but to make up forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not the first time, probably not the last time that we stumble over such subtleties or difficulties in translation. Perhaps you could give or read the word "reinforcement" in the original language, and the interpreters perhaps find another word than "reinforcement," the title of number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe Mr. Gorjanc should read the entire Article 118.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The units and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army and units, institutions, and staffs of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sure this is a well-meant proposal, but it's a long article, and what he -- the witness just has not read is what I wanted; namely, the title numbered 5, which is above Article 118. Just that title, if you please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Bringing units up to strength in the armed forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I grasp it now. Thank you. End of the interruption, Ms. Alaburic. Excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Article 118, it is confirmed that JNA units are brought up to strength with the men from the active and reserve forces; is that what we have just read?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All this is very well regulated by the Law on the Service in the Armed Forces. However, that document is not on our list. Let's look at the following document, which is 4D14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on, hold on. Witness, I have a follow-up question on the basis of that document. I was struck by the content of Article 12 on the role of the League of Communists in wartime. Under this Article 12, it plays a fundamental role, it's a driving force. Since you have known the Yugoslav system very well, and then you've also -- or you also know the system of your country, Slovenia, very well, could you tell me if, in your country, Slovenia, for example, or any country, in case of war, as regards the mindset and mentality of the country's inhabitants, is it the political party which is in power, which federates, coordinates, supports, the people's defence? On that basis in Herceg-Bosna, was it the role of HDZ HB to do this and to play that role which was carried out formerly by the League of Communists, but since it disappeared, is it a political -- a political party's role to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's very difficult for me to claim that. The League of Communists, in its programme, said that it was the leading political and ideological power of the Yugoslav society. As far as I know, there is no such provision in the HDZ, i.e., that it is the leading political power of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was some other parties present in the Croatian people and Croatians also belonged to some other parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it would be very difficult for me to determine or to draw that parallel between the League of Communists and the HDZ. However, I'm not excluding the possibility that at certain levels there may have been such attempts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the Law on Military Service. 4D1471 is the document number, 4D1471. The first article is Article number 47. This is the whole chapter in the law that regulates the obligation to serve in the reserve forces of the armed forces. Mr. Gorjanc, tell us, please, who was subject to that obligation to serve in the reserve forces of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't have that document here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, in which binder can I find that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm following the sequence of documents. I do have to say there has been some confusion. I am taking the document -- the documents one at a time in the sequence as they have been dispatched to my case manager. We are on the second binder. It is the first document in the second binder. This is what I've just been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, in my second binder the number of the first document is 4D01472. You have called 1471, so which one do you want? It's the number or the place, what we should rely on? The first document, to make it easier, is called "Decree on the Declaration of the Law on Service in the Armed Forces," and it is of February 1985, and the second one is dated "Belgrade, 1986," and is called "Law on Compulsory Military Service."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, document 4D1472 is the one that I have skipped because you have not allowed us to put it on our 65 ter list, and now I'm on document 4D1471, which is the second document in the sequence of documents in the second binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would now kindly ask the witness to -- I apologise for not having been aware of the fact that we have moved on to the second binder. I thought that we were on the first one. My mistake. In Article 47, the law prescribes who are those who are subject to serving in the reserve forces of the armed forces. Mr. Gorjanc, could you please tell us whose duty was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Of all those citizens of Yugoslavia who have completed their military service, also those who had regulated their military service in a different way, and also women conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Article 48, it is stipulated how long the obligation to serve in the reserve forces lasts. Mr. Gorjanc, could you please tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: From the day a person stopped his obligatory military service, and then in men up to the age of 60, and for women, from the ages of 19 to 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Article 69, there are provisions about the military records of military conscripts. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber as to how the military records were kept?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It was done on the territorial principle in municipalities, in the departments for All-People's Defence. In municipalities, I would like to say that in the year 1990 a decree came on the establishment of military districts, the military territorial commands, and then the records were taken over from the military departments of municipalities by the military districts and fell under the legal jurisdiction of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this part of your report, you talk about mobilisation. Could you please tell us about the forms of mobilisation that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Mobilisation could have been public or classified, general or individual, in the narrow sense of that term, it could be partial.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the end of that chapter, you refer us to a book by Gavro Perazic entitled "Constitutional, Political, International Legal Status of All-People's Defence and Armed Forces." Could you please tell us, Mr. Gorjanc -- we can find this in paragraph 62 of your report. Could you please explain to us who Gavro Perazic was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Professor Gavro Perazic, a colonel in the JNA, was one of the biggest experts on international laws of war in the former Yugoslavia. He authored several works about that subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understand his positions well, given the doctrine of All-People's Defence, he believes that a participant in the resistance is not only a person carrying arms and fighting, but also all those who do not carry arms but are potential fighters, which means that people who are members of the reserve forces, and, therefore, in case they are arrested, they should be treated as prisoners of war. Did I understand the whole point properly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, according to what you know and according to how you understand the rule -- regulations that prevailed at the time of the former Yugoslavia, is that how you saw the doctrine of All-People's Defence, and did you think that this was how it should have been applied?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let us now look at the application of the doctrine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general, paragraph 62 of your report is an interesting one, but I'm trying to figure out what exactly you meant. Let's take the case of a 30-year-old civilian who's not a member of any armed forces, but who's capable of holding a gun at some stage. Can that person or must that person be detained on the grounds that he's a potential enemy, and if arrested, what's his status? Is he a prisoner of war, or a combatant and, hence, has the status of a war prisoner, or is it a potentially -- or is it potentially a civilian who can be a combatant, and could he possibly refer the matter to any authority or to any court? Could you -- it is a complex matter, but I hope you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the Constitution and the laws, all those who put up resistance, irrespective of the fact whether they carry arms or not, are members of the armed forces. All those who have served in the army are military conscripts, irrespective of the facts whether they have been assigned to units or not. This means that if there is an indicia that such people who are not carrying arms and look like civilians, at first glance, if there are indicia that they might be detrimental, too, then they have to isolate it. Only in case that it is proven that they act in a detrimental way, they can be arrested. In any case, they enjoy the status of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an accurate answer, but I would like you to specify something. You said if there are indications, that person can be isolated. This is what you said, if there are indicia. Now, what does that mean, "isolate them," according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To isolate" means to restrict movement in a certain area or even within a person's place of residence, in their homes, placing them under house arrest or a special room that is monitored, under surveillance. I'm not talking about a POW camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And according to you, according to the surveys/studies carried out with an armed forces, or according to what you learned in the Military Academy, do these people have rights, these people who are isolated, or is it so that the only right they have is to remain silent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're a POW.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, still on paragraph 62, this last sentence is not quite clear for me. First you say if he, that is, a man in serviceable age, is not found in open, armed combat, the enemy should consider these men fit for military service. Are you sure you want to say "should" here? If you say "could," "might," I would understand, but do you state a duty for the enemy here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this case I'm quoting Colonel Perazic. Nevertheless, I personally believe that this is offered as a possibility, not an obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: All right. Then there is -- the language is not quite clear. And furthermore, you say "because in a different situation, they could be found bearing weapons." You establish here a relationship of causality. I must confess that I don't see any logic in this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All able-bodied men and other citizens are under an obligation to put up resistance. If they can get hold of arms, they are certainly expected to use those arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will not insist on this, bearing in mind that you're not a lawyer and you do not formulate along the way lawyers would expect -- be expected to. Thank you. Sorry, for the record, the last sentence, I'm speaking "would be expected to." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in your country, have you been personally faced with that same problem by which you isolated potential enemies or have you never been faced with that particular circumstance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, Your Honour, over in Slovenia I never encountered a situation like that. The armed clashes went on for a mere ten days over there. Nevertheless, the Slovenian authorities and the army, the Territorial Defence and police, were arresting JNA officers, taking them to prisoner camps, even arresting some in their homes and taking them away from their families in order to take them to these prisoner camps. One of these camps was in a coal mine over in Hrastnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You provide an example, the conflict lasted for ten days. But as far as you know, has the Slovenian Army arrested Serbs who were not JNA officers, but who were Serbs and who could potentially pose a threat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not as far as I know, but they had under their control most citizens hailing from other republics who were believed not to be loyal to these newly-established Slovenian authorities. That is why those people were erased from the register of citizens of the state of Slovenia, and as a consequence those people had to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, let us return to this document, the excerpt from Gavro Perazic's book, 4D1492. In response to Judge Trechsel's question, you said you were, in actual fact, quoting Mr. Perazic specifically in Article 62 of your expert report. Could we please, then, pay close attention to the following sentence which I'm about to read. It's at the very bottom of page 200: "If they were not caught in open armed struggle, the enemy can consider them to be potential fighters or combatants, and that is how they shall be treated, because in another situation they might be caught with weapons in their hands." While quoting Perazic, did you believe these people to also be potential combatants and that they should be treated as such, potential soldiers of an enemy army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. That wraps up this chapter, and we are now moving on to All-People's Defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the application of All-People's Defence. Let us look at what the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina has to say about this. It's a new chapter. It's in binder 2, 1D1236. You refer to this in paragraph 64 of your report. What we're dealing with is Article 162. Article 162, paragraph 3, reads: "Every citizen who, with arms or otherwise, participates in resistance to the aggressor shall be considered a member of the armed forces of the republic." Mr. Gorjanc, you can focus on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just say one thing? I don't have the transcript on my monitor. Therefore, I'm no longer able to follow the pace and when I should start answering.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now you have it on your screen. Could you please look at Article 162, paragraph 3. I've just quoted from it. I'm not going to repeat. Tell us, Mr. Gorjanc, do you see any difference between the definition in the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and what we saw as having been prescribed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your opinion and in your understanding of this provision, are the armed and unarmed resistance against an aggressor, are they one and the same, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, which is the Decree on Defence. This is 4D408. It is already in evidence, and we will not dwell upon this document for long. I would just like to highlight some parts that might be of some importance for the topic of All-People's Defence. In Article 5, line 3 or bullet point 3, a reference is made about resistance of people during the war. In Yugoslav regulations, reference is made to all-people's resistance. In your view, from a military perspective, is there any difference between the two terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: No, there is no difference. It's just about the wording.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 46, where reference is made to the rights and obligations of citizens in terms of defence. Mr. Gorjanc, we looked at the Yugoslav regulations and we saw that the defence of the country was right and the obligation of all citizens. Was the situation the same in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 48. Could you please tell us whether Article 48 speaks about work obligation? Was work obligation one of the forms of non-armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it could be understood. Units of work obligation were very often directly engaged on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How old did you have to be in order to fall under work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It started at the age of 15 and lasted until the age of 60. However, in mobilisation call-up papers, I often saw that work obligation extended up to the age of 65.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 66. Mr. Gorjanc, could you please help us to understand this article properly? I'm going to be very brief. This is about the deployment of human and material resources, and the final part of the provision reads so that all human and material resources of the republic are utilised for defence, to the optimum of their professional and other abilities. Could you please take an example of a chemical engineer who is a top expert for explosives. Could you take that example and explain how, based on the provisions of this law, such person could be engaged in the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In any case, he had to be engaged either in the production of explosives or -- in the production of basic or raw materials for the production of explosives, or in the institutes for the development of new explosives, or in the depots where explosives and explosive materials were safeguarded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, if you were a commander in wartime, would you engage such an engineer who worked in a factory and supplied the enemy army? Would you consider such a person as a more dangerous enemy than a foot soldier on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 70. The entire chapter is entitled "Scope and Structure of Civil Defence." The previous chapter of the same law applies to military defence. I conclude, therefore, Mr. Gorjanc, there are two basic types of defence, military and civil defence. Is that the way I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Article 71, there is the description of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm still a bit puzzled about this chemist who you have said, Mr. Gorjanc, that he's obliged to work on explosives. Now, let's say he's engaged in working on fertiliser or another very essential product for agriculture. Who is deciding whether he's going to do this or whether he's going to another department of the factory or to another factory to work on explosives? Who is taking that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision is taken by the administrative and executive bodies who assess where he would be more needed. Maybe he would be needed in the production of fertilisers, because agricultural production is also very important for resistance and for supplying armed forces, but this is not within the purview of decision-making by military bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's quite logical, yes, and it is not his own task to decide. You have said, No, thank you, or you have gestured, No, thank you. Ms. Alaburic, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just to come back to a doubt I have: We have this chemist who's working in a factory. Everyone knows that sometimes agricultural products may be used to make bombs. But independently from that, if the belligerent part considers that this chemist, this engineer, is a potential danger because of his knowledge, of his know-how, in such a case may he be isolated, put aside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask you something. We know that you decided that only General Petkovic's Defence will be entitled to examine Mr. Gorjanc. However, since Mr. Gorjanc is a joint expert used by both Praljak and Petkovic Defence, we would kindly ask you to take off from our time, if this is deemed to be necessary, by General Praljak's Defence, that you should allow General Praljak's Defence to put some questions, if, with your leave, General Praljak has one question to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I have to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber sees no problem, but on two conditions. First of all, that the time spent will be deducted from your time, and then General Praljak has to tell us what is the purpose of the question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just for the sake of clarification, the question concerns prisoners of war. In current war and after the Second World War, whether those were rocket scientists, chemists, physicists, in Germany it was Heisenberg, or, for example, in Russia, where engineers were being taken away, in that sense I wanted to ask Mr. Gorjanc -- and maybe I would have a few more questions by way of clarification, with your leave. So my first question is: Who may be considered a prisoner of war, for example, in the Second World War, in the Vietnam War, and so on and so forth? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about that category of people, a chemist in this particular case, I can provide an example from the Second World War. Engineers, Slovenians, were arrested as civilians by the German occupying forces, and they were taken to camps where they continued working as engineers in chemical plants and institutes. After the war, in 1948 they were sentenced as collaborators and traitors by the Slovenian government. And as for the other militaries in other wars, war prisoners were all those who were found with arms in their hands and also those who didn't carry arms. There were all sorts of types of isolation during different wars. For example, in the Second World War, after the attack by the Japanese Imperial Army against Pearl Harbor, all or nearly all citizens, irrespective of their age and sex, who were American citizens were incarcerated, if that is any sort of clarification that the general is satisfied with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I propose that I should finish this line of questioning the way I intended to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I wonder how you know this. Were the Americans -- were the Japanese arrested in the United States after Pearl Harbor, were they prisoners of war, according to your view, and in the sense of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know that. I apologise. I don't know, because I could only draw that knowledge from movies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will not press you on this. I think it's totally irrelevant, and you are not supposed to be an expert on the Law of War. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will go back to Article 66 in this law in the follow-up to Judge Trechsel's questions as to who would decide where the hypothetical engineer would be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, let's look at Article 66. What does Article 66 say? Who will take the decision on deployment of such people? What did you say? Who is it who decides about the assignment of such people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It is the civilian authorities, upon the request, for example, of companies that need people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what is the basic criterion when it comes to the assignment, in view of this article?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Professionalism and capability to contribute towards resistance in the highest possible level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's look at Article 47, paragraph 3. It says that citizens should communicate urgently to the reporting centre or the state authorities any defence-related information they've learned or noticed. Tell us, Mr. Gorjanc, does this refer to the intelligence activities on the part of citizens?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This is about intelligence activities on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at document 4D1475. It's not the -- if it's not in the next -- in the sequence, then it is the one after. It is 4D1475. This is an order issued by the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BiH Army, dated March 1993. Let's look at the ending of the second bullet point. It says: "As a special task, maintain connections with our structures and sympathizers in temporarily-occupied territory." Could you please tell us, Mr. Gorjanc, whether that would be in the function of the exercise of the Intelligence Service on the part of the citizens?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at document 4D409. This is a Decree Law on the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Article 4, paragraph 3, speaks about the bringing up to strength of war institutions and units. Mr. Gorjanc, how was this done in Bosnia-Herzegovina? How were war units brought up to strength?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: War units were brought up to strength from the ranks of military conscripts who served in the army, military conscripts serving in the army, and other able-bodied men who regulated their army service in any different -- any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this refer to reservists?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about the reserve composition, save for the conscripts who were serving in the army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: People who were reservists, were they also potential combatants?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When they became actual combatant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: When they were deployed into units and when they started carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the following decree, 4D412. This is the Decree on Service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's look at the decree law just briefly. Article 3, paragraph 1, defines the term of military personnel serving in the army, and Article 4, paragraph 2, speaks about soldiers and persons in the reserve force which -- who enter into service within the army. Mr. Gorjanc, tell us, please, persons in the reserve force, what is the basis for them entering into the army service? Is that their army obligation or some other obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Based on their army obligation upon a mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 60. This is about health-care, but we would like to see how the legislator differentiates between certain categories. In view of this provision, Mr. Gorjanc, would you say that there is a difference between army members and members of the armed forces during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. And now I would like us to look at document 1D1238. These are the amendments to the Decree Law on Defence. Let's look at Article 4. Actually, I'm going to skip this document altogether because there is no need to look at it. I wanted to draw your attention to other courier tasks and other tasks this decree defines. They're also members of the armed forces, people who act as couriers, what do they do exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The Defence Department in every municipality had the courier service which carried mobilisation call-up papers and other information to military conscripts. Those were people who were members of the staff of the Department of Defence or, alternatively, military conscripts who were not assigned to any units, but were still present on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness has just said, Your Honours, is regulated by Article 126(C) of this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 114 of your report, sir, contains a conclusion as to whether, under the BH regulations, the doctrine of All-People's Defence was, in fact, applied. Could you please outline your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the totality of laws and regulations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all citizens had the right and duty to participate in the country's defence and to directly contribute to its success in various ways, regardless of their age group, sex, or social status. In practical terms, the entire population was placed under the banner of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We've looked at the regulations, and could we now go and look at individual decisions and orders, showing how, if at all, this doctrine was implemented. The first document that I'd like to discuss with you is 4D403 which is a decision on the organisation of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you please explain about item 1? There is a distinction there between staffs and commands. Could you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This was adopted from the organisation of Yugoslavia's Territorial Defence, where they had staffs at various levels and unit commands within the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you to look at the types of tasks they were performing and to draw, based on that, a distinction between the staffs and commands, what would that difference be, the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In the erstwhile Territorial Defence, the staffs were in actual fact commands. They were only called staffs. I assume that the distinction here is provided based on the erstwhile doctrine. I'm not sure what time or period it dates back to.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: That means that they based the whole thing on the erstwhile structure of territorial defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at item 2, please. The Main Staff of the Armed Forces is classified as a staff and not a command. What would you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This a direct transfer from the erstwhile structure. The staffs were, in actual fact, commands over units. The units were the corps, the divisions, the brigades, the regiments. As far as the corps is concerned, I don't think there could have been any talk of that back in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, that far back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You have told us that the staffs, in actual fact, were performing the tasks of commands; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then why do we see commands as a special separate structure here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I'd be hard put to answer that question. I think this was copied from the erstwhile system of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next one up, P274, 274, the decision to declare a state of war. Paragraph 2 defines, as one of the objectives, the following: "A more efficient involvement of all human and material potentials." And paragraph 3 talks about organising all-people's resistance. In your opinion, Mr. Gorjanc, does this have anything to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, 4D1164, 4D1164. This is an order to declare a general public mobilisation in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Based on paragraph 1, who was it that was mobilised as a result of this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: All men of military age, between 18 and 55 years of age. Further, all citizens, men between 18 and 65 years of age, and women between 18 and 55 years of age, in terms of their respective war assignments, civil protection and other defence-related activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Talking about the first group you mentioned, men, men liable for military duty, does that refer to men who were in the reserve?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: All those liable, because there wasn't the textbook structure. It was only being set up, and they needed to draw up military records for that purpose. As I said, most of the records had been taken over from the JNA through the military districts, and one needed to establish a whole new set of military records to be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 says that any failure to adhere to this order would entail criminal and other responsibility under conditions of a state of war. Based on what you know about the laws that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia and at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what punishments were envisaged for a crime of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This was a misdemeanor, and this is described in greater detail in each of the provisions. And then there were certain punishments that were imposed under the Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D1727. This is a directive on the defence of sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated April 1992, signed by Hasanefendic, who was then commander, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question. In document 4D1164, one sees that women may also be considered as taking part in the territory of defence, the territorial defence. Could you tell me what is your point of view on the following situation? A woman who is wearing a camouflage uniform is cooking either in barracks for soldiers or on the ground. According to you, this woman, is she a soldier or civilian personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If she is within the barracks and cooking for soldiers there, then she's performing a task within that military unit and is, therefore, to be considered a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if she's in the field with the unit, is she carrying out a military mission or is she a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She's on a military mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, 4D1727, paragraph 2, says that forces of the Territorial Defence and armed civilians should be united under a single command. Getting people together like this and placing them under a single command, is something like this anything that has to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, fully. It's entirely consistent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, where it talks about stage 1, armed resistance by citizens on a massive scale, does this have anything to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, set up units of the TO, volunteer units, the Patriotic League, TO units, and other patriotic forces throughout the municipality, does this have anything to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Kim West for the Office of the Prosecution. Good afternoon to everyone else in and around the courtroom. Ms. Alaburic has been very pristine in her questions and have almost all have been open-ended questions. However, in the last ten minutes, and I understand that she's trying to get through some documents, there have been a number of leading questions, and I would just ask that they remain open-ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleague, and I fully agree with her objection and her remark. It was entirely my fault. I had failed to preface this by saying how I was going to examine the witness on this particular subject. I'll be asking about certain components of this document, and depending on his answers, I'll be asking an open-ended question at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If that is not consistent with the doctrine of All-People's Defence, why, and how, precisely, if it's inconsistent with the doctrine, why not? If it is, yes, and if it's not, why not? Could we just go through the document with these brief questions, simple questions, and clarify the whole thing eventually at the very end? If we could go to paragraph 6.2, Mr. Gorjanc, gathering intelligence involved one's own forces and equipment, MUP forces, loyal citizens, and local inhabitants, are we looking at intelligence that is part of the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. Witness, I wanted to ask a question earlier on, and I didn't, but I would like to take advantage of the consideration of 6.2 to ask the following question. In your CV, I saw that you had been an intelligence officer for a short period of time during your career in the JNA. As an intelligence officer, at the time whilst exercising your duty, were you in plain clothes or dressed with a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the division staff in Postojna, I was in charge of reconnaissance units within that division, the scouts, their training and their potential involvement in the eventuality of war. I was a military man. I was not a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So you always wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Day 1 to the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm asking the question because sometimes some military people wear civilian clothes for intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's possible, particularly when one crosses over into enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I think now you need to clarify this. Were you with the Security Service in the army - Intelligence Service, that's what it would translate into - or in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel please repeat this question. The interpreter did not understand the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The interpreters have not understood your question, Ms. Alaburic, even though, of course, the witness has. But it would be nice if you could repeat it, and then the witness would answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is hard to do an interpretation when there is too much interference between the two languages. The question should ideally be phrased either in Croatian or B/C/S or in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The SIS is the [In English] Security -- Intelligence Service, Security Service, Intelligence Service. [Interpretation] And if VOS, the military intelligence -- [In English] Military Informative Service. [Interpretation] Did you work for what resembled the SIS back in Yugoslavia or in the VOS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I was with the intelligence. It was called the Security Service or, as we called it, the KOS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that this right now is somewhat unclear to you, but I think it really is necessary to clarify this now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the KOS was the same thing as the SIS, would that mean that you were working with a service that, in Herceg-Bosna, was called the VOS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as the terminology is concerned, let me make this clear to everyone in the courtroom. I discussed this with our interpreters in order to be able to avoid confusion, because they use the word "intelligence," everything that we say about these services, and we concluded that the simplest thing might be to use the abbreviations SIS and VOS so we all know what we're talking about. The SIS and the VOS was the Military Intelligence Service that was within the Main Staff. It was a part of the Main Staff, and I don't think there should be any further problems understanding this. If my understanding is correct, we should take a break now. Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, but I'll give the floor to the Registrar for an IC number which was urgent.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Stojic Defence has submitted an objection to 4D list of exhibits with Witness Curcic. The document shall be given Exhibit IC1086.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, 1086, IC1086. Now a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's resume. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, the issue of somebody working in the KOS or not was a delicate issue in Slovenia, and after this confusion with terms, could you please tell us whether you ever worked in KOS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Never. I was not even an informer, a secret informer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We've clarified that. Let's go back to our document. In the meantime, I've decided to reduce the number of questions based on this document. Let me point you to Article 64. We're still on the same document, which is 4D1727, 4D1727.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Ms. Alaburic. You wanted to clarify something as regards the witness working or not with KOS, KOS being the intelligence -- the Military Intelligence Service within the Main Staff. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Nevertheless, it had its officers in units starting with battalions upwards. In every unit, there was a KOS officer or a KOS department. In a division, there was a department with several officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But you said that you didn't work for KOS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true. I never worked for KOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good, very well. So you worked for the counterpart of the SIS, but with a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not its counterpart. It was a decolent [as interpreted] of the Military Intelligence Service, also known as VOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is very complicated for us. As regards the service in which you worked, you said that it was the equivalent of VOS. But KOS, was it an equivalent of VOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were two completely different services, completely separate. KOS was in charge of internal security in the units and in the areas where the units were deployed. VOS or the Intelligence Service was active in collecting intelligence about a possible enemy, a possible opponent. KOS, on the other hand, collected intelligence about one's own forces, one's own officers, one's own territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I understand better now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, it stems from what you've just told us that in the Yugoslav People's Army, KOS was tied to the General Staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It played a dual role. While it was still KOS, until the year 1952, it was tied exclusively to the Ministry -- or, rather, the State Secretariat for National Defence. Later on, for a while it was tied to the General Staff or, rather, its Administration for Security, and for the last ten years or so - I can't tell you exactly for how long - it was again the Administration for Security that was subordinated to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and the Ministry of Defence. And maybe I can simplify things for you. It was a state within the state of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did KOS also control the moral and political suitability of the officers, their loyalty, their behaviour in private life?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It was its basic, fundamental duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you were once or at some point in time the subject of KOS activities and surveillance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am correcting the interpretation. My question was whether you were an object, [In English] object, [Interpretation] of KOS activities and surveillance. [In English] Okay, maybe it's a good translation. I don't know. I thought that maybe it's not, so I apologise if it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would suggest the word "target."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe that this would be the best interpretation. But the most important thing is that we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I would like to draw your attention to Article 6.4 of the same directive, where reference is made to all the other subjects in the territory that are duty-bound to work on the securing facilities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this have anything to do with All-People's Defence? Could you please provide the whole of the document from the point of view of All-People's Defence? Does it have anything to do with All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This is an example of how the doctrine was operationalised by way of a directive to engage military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, which is 1D942, 942. This is a platform for the activities of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in conditions of war. Please, let's first look at paragraph 5 of this document, which speaks about the political basis of the All-People's Defence war. In the second line, a reference is made to the All-People's Defence war of all citizens and all peoples, aimed at liberating Bosnia-Herzegovina. In your understanding of the doctrine of All-People's Defence, does this have anything to do with that doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the paragraph 6 of the same document. An appeal is to launch to all patriots and all citizens in Bosnia-Herzegovina to actively join the patriotic front. This appeal to all citizens, does this have anything to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at the following document, which is 4D1240, 4D1240. I am repeating the document number, 4D1240. This is a directive issued by the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated September 1992. The document has several significant parts and several important claims. Irrespective of the topic that we are covering. At the moment, I would like us to look at the entire document. On page 1, Mr. Gorjanc, could you please look at the definition of aggressor as the combined forces of the armed forces of Serbia and Montenegro, the rump of the former JNA, and so on and so forth, and it says here that the aggressor is preparing actions by which it wants to separate the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Republic of Croatia. Would your personal knowledge about the plans of the activities of the JNA in that territory point to the fact that there was, indeed, such a goal even during the time when the JNA was functioning?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that was in case of an attack from the West?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, for the aggression from the West or, to be more precise, in the case of the NATO forces landing in the territory of Central Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you -- using one of the maps, did you depict that planned activity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I illustrated the plan of a possible engagement of the forces of my corps that had been elaborated in February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This was still a JNA corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA corps from Uzice, which is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at number 3 on page 3, Mr. Gorjanc. This is how neighbours of the armed forces were defined, and we're talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I quote: "The Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia engaged in the offensive activities for the liberation of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, some part of the forces engaged in the territory of Dubrovnik will cooperate closely with our forces in an effort to liberate East Herzegovina and particularly the towns of Trebinje and Stolac ..." If this document was signed by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what would you then conclude? Is he talking about the joint, synchronised activities undertaken on the part of the armies of the two states?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This document shows that this was, indeed, a joint action of two allies, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say in the function of two allies working together, could you please repeat your answer, because the end of the sentence was not interpreted. You said that this shows that their cooperation was in the function of the two of them working as allies, to say the least?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I can't claim, based on this document, this was a coordinated, joint action, because there should have been a special staff that would be in control and command of such a joint action, if that, indeed, was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Irrespective of the degree of cooperation, it is indisputable that it was cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It was a joint activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at bullet point 4, second paragraph. It says: "Main forces to be engaged on lifting the blockade of Sarajevo to liberate -- to defend liberated territories and for defensive activities." My question to you, Mr. Gorjanc, is this: If the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was planning an action to lift the blockade of the city of Sarajevo, according to your knowledge of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what territory should have the BiH Army have had complete control of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: In order to lift the blockade of the city of Sarajevo, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina should have had full control of the territory of Mount Igman, the territory of Konjic, and the territory of North Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look under 5; tasks, operational forces, in connection with the 4th Corps. That's on page 4. Certain activities are planned in cooperation with the forces of the Republic of Croatia. Could you please explain the cooperation with the forces of the Republic of Croatia, could you say something about the degree of that cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This term, "sadestvo" [phoen] is a higher form of cooperation. This immediate cooperation and joint combat activity in one and the same facility or against one and the same target of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at number 6, "Content of Armed Combat," where it says "Sabotage and Anti-Sabotage Combat." This is on page 7 of the B/C/S text, and here reference is made to continuous conduct of large-scale sabotage operations in the aggressor's rear. Could you please explain, Mr. Gorjanc, this term "aggressor's rear," what area is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The aggressor's rear depends on the size of the unit that is engaged on the front-line, and the views of that are different in different armies. In the army that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the rear meant the area behind the first line of defence, which was three to five kilometres from the contact line or contact point with the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, this kind of planning of sabotage warfare as an important element of combat, does it have anything to do with All-People's Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This is completely and fully in the spirit of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at Chapter 7, under "Intelligence Service" or "Intelligence Support." This is on your page 8. It says: "The task of intelligence support will engage intelligence bodies and reconnoitering units, the MUP forces, and the population." Mr. Gorjanc, could you comment upon the engagement of the population within this context?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The population is deployed across the entire territory, and the population can continuously observe the situation as it evolves on the territory. The only question is: To what degree is the population organised in order to convey the results of their observation of the territory as quickly as possible? In the former state, within the concept of All-People's Defence and the gathering of intelligence about the enemy, there was a special service, the so-called Local Reconnoitering and Intelligence Service. Military intelligence officers would engage or hire reliable members of the population who gathered intelligence, and they, in their turn, spread their network further afield.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at a chapter called "Logistics as Support." Let's look at the quarter-master's support. This is on your page 9. Could you please tell us, when it comes to food supply, accommodation, the possibilities of maintaining hygiene, does this have anything to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, because it relies fully on the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were I to ask you now about this document in its entirety, was this document prepared in terms of having anything to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence, what could you tell us as a general clarification?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It's a textbook example of how the doctrine of All-People's Defence was operationalised, in terms of a military order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, Mr. Gorjanc. This is 4D1603, 1603, 1603. That's right. Page 1, paragraph 1.1: "The unity of all components of armed struggle and resistance." Paragraph 2: "The unity of the army and the people must be fostered and boosted through all various forms of preparing both the army and the people to defend the country." There is mention there of all sorts of efforts being made by the people to help the army; manifested in its financial security, care for the sick and wounded, gathering information on the enemy, uncovering and obstructing enemy agents, securing important features, participation in fortification of the terrain, and other activities. Mr. Gorjanc, what about this definition and these tasks; does that have anything to do with the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. On to the last document, in terms of this whole, 4D766, proposed measures to organise All-People's Defence war. Paragraph 2 and the first line in paragraph 1: "Maximum mobilisation of all segments and potentials of the state to ensure its survival." The bullet that I mentioned: "At this crucial hour, we must organise all political forces, parties, associations, movements, and citizens to form a patriotic front." Can you comment on this document from the perspective of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: It is fully in the spirit of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At 6.3 of your expert report, you talk about actions in the enemy rear by relying on the population. This is one of the elements of the doctrine of All-People's Defence. You told us about what "the rear" meant in this case, and could I please ask you to explain, why is this considered a part of the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Simply because this activity in the enemy's rear was particularly important in terms of inflicting the losses and damage on the enemy, and leaving the enemy in disarray, reducing the pressure along the front-line and raising the morale of one's own forces, raising the morale of one's own forces and the population on either side of the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now 4D1476, the next document. This is an order by the 306th Mountain Brigade belonging to the 3rd BH Army Corps, January 1993, securing rural areas. Paragraph 2 reads: "Involve all able-bodied residents to secure the villages in which they live. All conscripts, regardless of whether they have work obligation or are battalion members, on condition that they are free, are to be involved." Can you comment on this from the perspective of involving population not directly on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Under the doctrine, the entire population was committed to establishing a level of security to ensure that the units involved in military actions got enough rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on this document, it would follow that a commander of the BH Army was determining what tasks military conscripts would have, those who were not in the army. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, to form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, be careful, be prudent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just introducing the question. I didn't actually ask my question yet. I was just stating that this was an order by a military commander of the BH Army which establishes what military conscripts were to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, could you please comment on this? How is it possible for a commander of the army to determine and decide how military conscripts should be involved in activities in certain villages and towns?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I suppose there were no functioning civilian authorities in place in these areas, no police providing security. In order to establish a security system, he had to do this himself. I happen to know that this was in the immediate vicinity of the front-line on the eastern slopes of Mount Vlasic, in the immediate vicinity of the Serb forces that were there. It was only logical for him to do that, and under the doctrine he was definitely allowed to take those steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say the doctrine allowed him to take those steps, what exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I mean all military conscripts, regardless of whether they were deployed to military units, were duty-bound to respond to any call-up to perform their military duties. In this specific case, this entailed security.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document that I have prepared for you -- or, rather, a set of three documents should be an example of acts of sabotage that were carried out. Of course, you can't address this from a factual perspective, or at least not in detail, but perhaps you could comment on 4D462, 4D462, which is an official transcript or record reflecting an interview. The interviewee was Salko Alihodzic. He describes actions taken by the population and organised by the BH Army in Dubravska Plateau in mid-July 1993. Please look at the document and tell us whether it has anything to do with acts of sabotage carried out under the doctrine of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I happen to be familiar with this area. I know for a fact that the area was HVO controlled at the time. There were no BH Army units around. This is not a textbook act of sabotage, in terms of penetrating behind enemy lines in order to carry out sabotage. It is my conviction that this gentleman was probably keeping a rifle at his home. Someone then simply called him, and he joined this action. But it wasn't the unit, as such, in this case that was organised to perform this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D910, 910. Likewise, an official record. The interviewee here is Musair Klaric, describing the very same event. In paragraph 2, he says that all of this was happening based on a scenario devised by the BH Army in the area of Dubrava. Can you comment on this, Mr. Gorjanc, in the overall context of these documents and what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I could say that this -- this is basically about ad hoc training and establishment of BH Army units at someone's request. He says, There were very few of us at the beginning, but later we grew to become a group of about 120 men, weapons were then distributed, and so on and so forth, which means that weapons had been hidden somewhere previously. You couldn't simply carry weapons across arms, especially not in these quantities, and still pass unobserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The last document of this set is 4D1730, the last document in this set. Let me draw your attention to a set of proposed measures. I'm talking about item -- paragraph 14, which is page 4 in your copy, sir. I will read, and you can simply listen because it's simple enough. The task is as follows: "Continue to insert, on an even larger scale, sabotage groups in the enemy's rear in order to carry out acts of sabotage or commando raids." Could you comment on this from the perspective of acts of sabotage as part of the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, it's fully consistent with the most salient premises of the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next document, then. Let me just take a minute to sort the documents out. The next paragraph is in relation to Chapter 7 of your report. The issue is Muslim soldiers as a potential security problem. To begin with, Mr. Gorjanc, we should look at three maps on our screens. The first map is 4D1216, 4D1216, which is a map of Mostar up until the 30th of June, 1993. You see, Mr. Gorjanc -- do you see the East Mostar area here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the blue portions? That marks the positions of the HVO? What would you say? Up until the 30th of June, 1993, who is it that is in control of the areas to the north and south of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. 4D561, the next map. As a matter of fact, I don't have a question about that map. Let's move on to the next one, 4D562, just these two maps for you to see what was going on further north from East Mostar in Central Bosnia. We'll put all of these together at a later date. You've seen these maps before, and there's no need for us to dwell on them any longer now. Let's first try to see if the HVO had any inkling whatsoever that the BH Army was planning to take the whole Neretva River Valley. The first document is 4D948. Sir, this is an order by the Chief of the Main Staff, dated the 7th of June, 1993. Looking at this, could we conclude that the HVO knew anything about the BH Army being about to launch offensive operations in the areas of Jablanica, Bijelo Polje, and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: This shows that the HVO was taking some preemptive measures in the expectation that the BH Army would be launching offensive operations throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D702, 702, the letter by the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. The date is the 30th of June, 1993, after the BH Army had seized control of the territory to the north of East Mostar. The date is the 30th of June, 1993. The letter was sent to Mr. Wahlgren and Mr. Morillon. Paragraph 6 reads, I quote: "We would like to remind you that during the meeting with General Morillon in Medjugorje on June 26th, 1993, our side warned about the possibility that the Muslim side was organising a frontal assault against the town of Mostar, the HVO positions, and its surroundings." The next paragraph claims that this was very easy to foresee and was logical as a continuation of offensive activities by the Muslim forces that had begun in Central Bosnia and then later continued in Northern Herzegovina: "The Mostar Valley and the whole of Neretva Valley are only a continuation of the same geo-strategic entity across which the Muslim leadership wanted to gain access to the sea." My first question to you, Mr. Gorjanc, you being someone who is knowledgeable about the geographical setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is it true that the Mostar Valley and the entire Neretva Valley are a continuation of the same geo-strategic entity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: That is entirely true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Looking at this document, could you, too, conclude that the HVO knew about these offensive operations that were being planned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: Yes, they sure knew about this. We know that because they warned the UNPROFOR commander for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, let's imagine we're facing the following situation, we have the following premises: Firstly, the HVO units in the area contained a large percentage of Muslims. The HVO units in the area contained a large percentage of Muslims. Secondly, up until that point in time, no special steps had been taken against the Muslim soldiers in the HVO, in terms of a precaution, in terms of being disarmed, or isolated. Given your vast knowledge and experience, what would you be led to conclude about the relationship between the HVO military commanders and their Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: There are two possibilities. Either they were not careful, which I very much doubt because they had even gone so far as to warn international players about this possibility and have given their units' tasks that were aimed at stopping precisely this. I think the intention and the general will was to maintain these relations at a good level of cooperation and to continue to work as allies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I asked you specifically about the Muslim soldiers in the HVO, who were members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: I believe that the HVO commanders did trust those men, after all, probably knowing most of them on a personal basis, and they had been fighting head to head with the Croat soldiers from the same units for at least six or seven months previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, looking at this point in time, late June, if you had been an HVO commander in the area and if you had known about these plans and operations being in the offing by the BH Army, if you had even suspected that there was a possibility for Muslim soldiers not to remain loyal to you, would you have taken any measures, and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC
utterances.text: The first measure I would have taken would have been to establish surveillance, especially concerning officers in higher levels of command, and units that were predominantly Muslim.
